phase_label: Phase 2: LLM Engineer, MLOps Engineer, ML Platform Engineer, Data Engineer for ML
intended_use: Detailed self-study reading materials aligned to the role/topic inventory used for the 12,000-question MCQ/MSQ bank.

schema.topics: Each topic module contains learning objectives, detailed reading notes, practice tasks, pitfalls, and mastery checks.
schema.source_question_count: Number of questions in the original bank for this role/topic.

roles.role_mission: design, fine-tune, evaluate, and serve large language model systems with attention to context, alignment, throughput, and failure modes
roles.quality_bar: LLM behavior is measurable, controllable, secure, efficient, and robust across languages, tasks, and adversarial inputs
reading_strategy: Read the first pass for vocabulary and assumptions.
Read the second pass by building a small artifact for each topic.
For every topic, write one failure mode, one diagnostic, one stakeholder caveat, and one production or governance implication.
Treat medium questions as application checks and hard questions as failure-mode, tradeoff, and design-reasoning checks.

topics.learning_objective: Master multi-turn memory well enough to apply it in the LLM Engineer role: define the assumptions, choose the right method or design, detect subtle failure modes, and explain tradeoffs to technical and non-technical stakeholders.
topics.overview: This module treats multi-turn memory as a medium-to-hard job skill for a LLM Engineer. Read it through the lens of model internals, inference mechanics, prompt/tool contracts, and evaluation discipline. The goal is not memorization; it is being able to reason from first principles, audit edge cases, and produce artifacts such as fine-tuning run, serving stack, tool schema.
topics.role_application: For a LLM Engineer, multi-turn memory matters because the role's mission is to design, fine-tune, evaluate, and serve large language model systems with attention to context, alignment, throughput, and failure modes. The expected quality bar is that LLM behavior is measurable, controllable, secure, efficient, and robust across languages, tasks, and adversarial inputs. When answering interview questions or doing project work, connect multi-turn memory to a real artifact and a measurable decision.
reading_path: Define the exact problem statement for multi-turn memory: inputs, outputs, users, decision point, and failure cost.
Write the assumptions that must hold for multi-turn memory to be valid in a realistic LLM Engineer workflow.
Study the mechanics using a small worked example, then deliberately break the example with edge cases.
Map diagnostics and quality checks to concrete artifacts: tests, dashboards, evaluation tables, runbooks, or decision memos.
Summarize the tradeoffs in one page: when to use the technique, when not to use it, and how to monitor it after launch.

reading_sections.title: Foundations
reading_sections.reading_note: Start from the user task and decide what the model should know, retrieve, infer, or refuse. Separate model capability from application architecture: prompts, retrieval, tools, memory, safety, and evaluation all shape behavior. While studying multi-turn memory, keep a running list of assumptions, failure cases, and the evidence needed before using it in production or decision-making.

reading_sections.title: Mechanics
reading_sections.reading_note: Study chunking, embeddings, hybrid retrieval, reranking, context packing, decoding, tool schemas, structured output, fine-tuning, and preference optimization. Understand when RAG, fine-tuning, prompting, or routing is the right lever. While studying multi-turn memory, keep a running list of assumptions, failure cases, and the evidence needed before using it in production or decision-making.

reading_sections.title: Evaluation
reading_sections.reading_note: Measure groundedness, factuality, task success, refusal behavior, safety, latency, cost, and regression across prompt/model versions. Include adversarial and multi-turn cases, not just happy-path examples. While studying multi-turn memory, keep a running list of assumptions, failure cases, and the evidence needed before using it in production or decision-making.

reading_sections.title: Security and safety
reading_sections.reading_note: Treat prompts and retrieved content as untrusted input. Build defenses against prompt injection, data exfiltration, tool misuse, privacy leakage, and overconfident unsupported answers. While studying multi-turn memory, keep a running list of assumptions, failure cases, and the evidence needed before using it in production or decision-making.

practice_lab.title: Applied lab: multi-turn memory for LLM Engineer
practice_lab.setup: Create a realistic mini-scenario where a LLM Engineer must make or defend a decision involving multi-turn memory.
tasks: Create the minimum dataset, architecture sketch, experiment plan, rubric, or policy artifact needed to reason about multi-turn memory.
Introduce two edge cases that would mislead a superficial solution for multi-turn memory.
Write the checks or metrics that would catch those edge cases before a decision, launch, or handoff.
Prepare a short stakeholder explanation that includes assumptions, tradeoffs, and residual risk.
practice_lab.deliverable: A concise artifact proving you can apply multi-turn memory: one table, diagram, query, evaluation report, runbook, or decision memo plus a paragraph of caveats.

practice_drills: build a RAG eval with retrieval and answer-level metrics
design a function-calling schema with validation and authorization checks
create a prompt regression suite with benign, edge, and adversarial cases
common_pitfalls: using fine-tuning to solve a missing-knowledge problem better handled by retrieval
evaluating RAG only by generation quality while ignoring retrieval recall
letting retrieved text override system or developer instructions
treating LLM-as-judge scores as objective without calibration
mastery_check: Explain multi-turn memory without using buzzwords, including the assumptions and what can go wrong.
Given a messy scenario, choose an appropriate method or design for multi-turn memory and justify it against at least two alternatives.
Design validation checks that would detect silent failure or misleading success for multi-turn memory.
Communicate the conclusion with uncertainty, limitations, and a next action.
assessment_prompts: What is the most dangerous hidden assumption in a typical use of multi-turn memory, and how would you test it?
How would your answer change if data volume, latency, privacy, or cost constraints became 10x tighter?
What metric or diagnostic would you distrust most for multi-turn memory, and what companion evidence would you require?

Separate model capability from application architecture: prompts, retrieval, tools, memory, safety, and evaluation all shape behavior. While studying safety alignment tradeoffs, keep a running list of assumptions, failure cases, and the evidence needed before using it in production or decision-making.

reading_sections.title: Mechanics
reading_sections.reading_note: Study chunking, embeddings, hybrid retrieval, reranking, context packing, decoding, tool schemas, structured output, fine-tuning, and preference optimization. Understand when RAG, fine-tuning, prompting, or routing is the right lever. While studying safety alignment tradeoffs, keep a running list of assumptions, failure cases, and the evidence needed before using it in production or decision-making.

reading_sections.title: Evaluation
reading_sections.reading_note: Measure groundedness, factuality, task success, refusal behavior, safety, latency, cost, and regression across prompt/model versions. Include adversarial and multi-turn cases, not just happy-path examples. While studying safety alignment tradeoffs, keep a running list of assumptions, failure cases, and the evidence needed before using it in production or decision-making.

reading_sections.title: Security and safety
reading_sections.reading_note: Treat prompts and retrieved content as untrusted input. Build defenses against prompt injection, data exfiltration, tool misuse, privacy leakage, and overconfident unsupported answers. While studying safety alignment tradeoffs, keep a running list of assumptions, failure cases, and the evidence needed before using it in production or decision-making.

practice_lab.title: Applied lab: safety alignment tradeoffs for LLM Engineer
practice_lab.setup: Create a realistic mini-scenario where a LLM Engineer must make or defend a decision involving safety alignment tradeoffs.
tasks: Create the minimum dataset, architecture sketch, experiment plan, rubric, or policy artifact needed to reason about safety alignment tradeoffs.
Introduce two edge cases that would mislead a superficial solution for safety alignment tradeoffs.
Write the checks or metrics that would catch those edge cases before a decision, launch, or handoff.
Prepare a short stakeholder explanation that includes assumptions, tradeoffs, and residual risk.
practice_lab.deliverable: A concise artifact proving you can apply safety alignment tradeoffs: one table, diagram, query, evaluation report, runbook, or decision memo plus a paragraph of caveats.

practice_drills: build a RAG eval with retrieval and answer-level metrics
design a function-calling schema with validation and authorization checks
create a prompt regression suite with benign, edge, and adversarial cases
common_pitfalls: using fine-tuning to solve a missing-knowledge problem better handled by retrieval
evaluating RAG only by generation quality while ignoring retrieval recall
letting retrieved text override system or developer instructions
treating LLM-as-judge scores as objective without calibration
mastery_check: Explain safety alignment tradeoffs without using buzzwords, including the assumptions and what can go wrong.
Given a messy scenario, choose an appropriate method or design for safety alignment tradeoffs and justify it against at least two alternatives.
Design validation checks that would detect silent failure or misleading success for safety alignment tradeoffs.
Communicate the conclusion with uncertainty, limitations, and a next action.
assessment_prompts: What is the most dangerous hidden assumption in a typical use of safety alignment tradeoffs, and how would you test it?
How would your answer change if data volume, latency, privacy, or cost constraints became 10x tighter?
What metric or diagnostic would you distrust most for safety alignment tradeoffs, and what companion evidence would you require?

topics.learning_objective: Master multilingual LLM evaluation well enough to apply it in the LLM Engineer role: define the assumptions, choose the right method or design, detect subtle failure modes, and explain tradeoffs to technical and non-technical stakeholders.
topics.overview: This module treats multilingual LLM evaluation as a medium-to-hard job skill for a LLM Engineer. Read it through the lens of model internals, inference mechanics, prompt/tool contracts, and evaluation discipline. The goal is not memorization; it is being able to reason from first principles, audit edge cases, and produce artifacts such as fine-tuning run, serving stack, tool schema.
topics.role_application: For a LLM Engineer, multilingual LLM evaluation matters because the role's mission is to design, fine-tune, evaluate, and serve large language model systems with attention to context, alignment, throughput, and failure modes. The expected quality bar is that LLM behavior is measurable, controllable, secure, efficient, and robust across languages, tasks, and adversarial inputs. When answering interview questions or doing project work, connect multilingual LLM evaluation to a real artifact and a measurable decision.
reading_path: Define the exact problem statement for multilingual LLM evaluation: inputs, outputs, users, decision point, and failure cost.
Write the assumptions that must hold for multilingual LLM evaluation to be valid in a realistic LLM Engineer workflow.
Study the mechanics using a small worked example, then deliberately break the example with edge cases.
Map diagnostics and quality checks to concrete artifacts: tests, dashboards, evaluation tables, runbooks, or decision memos.
Summarize the tradeoffs in one page: when to use the technique, when not to use it, and how to monitor it after launch.

reading_sections.title: Foundations
reading_sections.reading_note: Study evaluation as a measurement system for release decisions. Define the capability, unacceptable failures, population slices, scoring rubric, required confidence, and action taken on failure. While studying multilingual LLM evaluation, keep a running list of assumptions, failure cases, and the evidence needed before using it in production or decision-making.

reading_sections.title: Mechanics
reading_sections.reading_note: Build golden sets, adversarial sets, regression suites, structured validators, human-eval rubrics, and telemetry sampling. Combine automated scoring with human review where judgment is required. While studying multilingual LLM evaluation, keep a running list of assumptions, failure cases, and the evidence needed before using it in production or decision-making.

reading_sections.title: Diagnostics
reading_sections.reading_note: Check leakage, annotator disagreement, benchmark contamination, metric gaming, LLM-judge bias, coverage gaps, false positive/negative costs, and offline-online correlation. Evaluation quality itself needs monitoring. While studying multilingual LLM evaluation, keep a running list of assumptions, failure cases, and the evidence needed before using it in production or decision-making.

reading_sections.title: Release use
reading_sections.reading_note: Tie eval results to gates: block, warn, launch with mitigations, or rollback. Quality engineering is strongest when thresholds are explicit before the result is known. While studying multilingual LLM evaluation, keep a running list of assumptions, failure cases, and the evidence needed before using it in production or decision-making.

The goal is not memorization; it is being able to reason from first principles, audit edge cases, and produce artifacts such as fine-tuning run, serving stack, tool schema.
topics.role_application: For a LLM Engineer, catastrophic forgetting matters because the role's mission is to design, fine-tune, evaluate, and serve large language model systems with attention to context, alignment, throughput, and failure modes. The expected quality bar is that LLM behavior is measurable, controllable, secure, efficient, and robust across languages, tasks, and adversarial inputs. When answering interview questions or doing project work, connect catastrophic forgetting to a real artifact and a measurable decision.
reading_path: Define the exact problem statement for catastrophic forgetting: inputs, outputs, users, decision point, and failure cost.
Write the assumptions that must hold for catastrophic forgetting to be valid in a realistic LLM Engineer workflow.
Study the mechanics using a small worked example, then deliberately break the example with edge cases.
Map diagnostics and quality checks to concrete artifacts: tests, dashboards, evaluation tables, runbooks, or decision memos.
Summarize the tradeoffs in one page: when to use the technique, when not to use it, and how to monitor it after launch.

reading_sections.title: Foundations
reading_sections.reading_note: Start from the user task and decide what the model should know, retrieve, infer, or refuse. Separate model capability from application architecture: prompts, retrieval, tools, memory, safety, and evaluation all shape behavior. While studying catastrophic forgetting, keep a running list of assumptions, failure cases, and the evidence needed before using it in production or decision-making.

reading_sections.title: Mechanics
reading_sections.reading_note: Study chunking, embeddings, hybrid retrieval, reranking, context packing, decoding, tool schemas, structured output, fine-tuning, and preference optimization. Understand when RAG, fine-tuning, prompting, or routing is the right lever. While studying catastrophic forgetting, keep a running list of assumptions, failure cases, and the evidence needed before using it in production or decision-making.

reading_sections.title: Evaluation
reading_sections.reading_note: Measure groundedness, factuality, task success, refusal behavior, safety, latency, cost, and regression across prompt/model versions. Include adversarial and multi-turn cases, not just happy-path examples. While studying catastrophic forgetting, keep a running list of assumptions, failure cases, and the evidence needed before using it in production or decision-making.

reading_sections.title: Security and safety
reading_sections.reading_note: Treat prompts and retrieved content as untrusted input. Build defenses against prompt injection, data exfiltration, tool misuse, privacy leakage, and overconfident unsupported answers. While studying catastrophic forgetting, keep a running list of assumptions, failure cases, and the evidence needed before using it in production or decision-making.

tasks: Create the minimum dataset, architecture sketch, experiment plan, rubric, or policy artifact needed to reason about cost allocation for GPU jobs.
Introduce two edge cases that would mislead a superficial solution for cost allocation for GPU jobs.
Write the checks or metrics that would catch those edge cases before a decision, launch, or handoff.
Prepare a short stakeholder explanation that includes assumptions, tradeoffs, and residual risk.
practice_lab.deliverable: A concise artifact proving you can apply cost allocation for GPU jobs: one table, diagram, query, evaluation report, runbook, or decision memo plus a paragraph of caveats.

practice_drills: profile a training run and identify the top bottleneck
estimate memory use for activations, parameters, gradients, and optimizer state
write a cost report comparing two training configurations
common_pitfalls: optimizing GPU kernels while the input pipeline is the bottleneck
improving mean latency while p95 gets worse
using mixed precision without monitoring numerical instability
ignoring checkpoint compatibility during distributed training changes
mastery_check: Explain cost allocation for GPU jobs without using buzzwords, including the assumptions and what can go wrong.
Given a messy scenario, choose an appropriate method or design for cost allocation for GPU jobs and justify it against at least two alternatives.
Design validation checks that would detect silent failure or misleading success for cost allocation for GPU jobs.
Communicate the conclusion with uncertainty, limitations, and a next action.
assessment_prompts: What is the most dangerous hidden assumption in a typical use of cost allocation for GPU jobs, and how would you test it?
How would your answer change if data volume, latency, privacy, or cost constraints became 10x tighter?
What metric or diagnostic would you distrust most for cost allocation for GPU jobs, and what companion evidence would you require?

roles.role_mission: build shared platforms that let many teams train, evaluate, deploy, monitor, and govern ML/AI systems safely at scale
roles.quality_bar: platform users can self-serve safely while the platform enforces reliability, security, cost, and governance controls
reading_strategy: Read the first pass for vocabulary and assumptions.
Read the second pass by building a small artifact for each topic.
For every topic, write one failure mode, one diagnostic, one stakeholder caveat, and one production or governance implication.
Treat medium questions as application checks and hard questions as failure-mode, tradeoff, and design-reasoning checks.

topics.learning_objective: Master autoscaling strategy well enough to apply it in the ML Platform Engineer role: define the assumptions, choose the right method or design, detect subtle failure modes, and explain tradeoffs to technical and non-technical stakeholders.
topics.overview: This module treats autoscaling strategy as a medium-to-hard job skill for a ML Platform Engineer. Read it through the lens of platform architecture, API design, multi-tenancy, scalability, and developer experience. The goal is not memorization; it is being able to reason from first principles, audit edge cases, and produce artifacts such as platform API, golden path template, multi-tenant serving layer.
topics.role_application: For a ML Platform Engineer, autoscaling strategy matters because the role's mission is to build shared platforms that let many teams train, evaluate, deploy, monitor, and govern ML/AI systems safely at scale. The expected quality bar is that platform users can self-serve safely while the platform enforces reliability, security, cost, and governance controls. When answering interview questions or doing project work, connect autoscaling strategy to a real artifact and a measurable decision.
reading_path: Define the exact problem statement for autoscaling strategy: inputs, outputs, users, decision point, and failure cost.
Write the assumptions that must hold for autoscaling strategy to be valid in a realistic ML Platform Engineer workflow.
Study the mechanics using a small worked example, then deliberately break the example with edge cases.
Map diagnostics and quality checks to concrete artifacts: tests, dashboards, evaluation tables, runbooks, or decision memos.
Summarize the tradeoffs in one page: when to use the technique, when not to use it, and how to monitor it after launch.

reading_sections.title: Foundations
reading_sections.reading_note: Study ML systems as production services with data dependencies, model artifacts, interfaces, SLOs, owners, and rollback procedures. reading_sections.title: Mechanics

While studying autoscaling strategy, keep a running list of assumptions, failure cases, and the evidence needed before using it in production or decision-making.

While studying autoscaling strategy, keep a running list of assumptions, failure cases, and the evidence needed before using it in production or decision-making.

While studying autoscaling strategy, keep a running list of assumptions, failure cases, and the evidence needed before using it in production or decision-making.
